## Environment

- Repository: `bloomberg/clang-p2996`
- Commit: `7220baffd57ea5b0f8cf59bee494dd5b7cc2b748`
- Version: `clang version 21.0.0git`
- Target: `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`
- Flags: `-freflection -std=c++2c`
- Toolchain: bundled libc++

## Reproducer

`repro_prefix.hpp`:

```cpp
#pragma once
#include <meta>

namespace n0 { struct Decl {}; }

namespace util {
struct FindResult {
    std::meta::info decl{};
    int decl_count{};
};

consteval FindResult FindMarker(std::meta::info Scope) {
    FindResult result{};
    result.decl_count = static_cast<int>(
        std::meta::members_of(Scope, std::meta::access_context::current()).size());
    return result;
}
} // namespace util
```

`repro_driver.cpp`:

```cpp
#include "repro_prefix.hpp"

static constexpr auto r = util::FindMarker(^^n0);
static_assert(r.decl_count == 1);
```

From the directory containing these files, set `T` to the clang-p2996
toolchain root and run:

```sh
T=/path/to/clang-p2996
clang="$T/bin/clang++"
common=(
  -freflection -std=c++2c -nostdinc++
  -I"$T/include/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/c++/v1"
  -I"$T/include/c++/v1"
  -resource-dir="$T/lib/clang/21"
)

# Textual inclusion succeeds.
"$clang" "${common[@]}" -c -o repro_driver-textual.o repro_driver.cpp

# PCH generation succeeds.
"$clang" "${common[@]}" -x c++-header --precompile \
  -o repro_prefix.hpp.pch repro_prefix.hpp

# Consuming the PCH crashes.
"$clang" "${common[@]}" -include-pch repro_prefix.hpp.pch \
  -c -o repro_driver-pch.o repro_driver.cpp
```

The first two commands exit 0. The final command segfaults in the frontend;
the outer driver exits 1 and reports:

```text
clang frontend command failed with exit code 139
```

Expected: consuming the PCH succeeds, as it does when the same header is
included textually.

Actual: consuming the PCH segfaults in the frontend.

The crash occurs while evaluating the initializer of `r`. The top relevant
frames are:

```text
EvaluateInPlace
EvaluateCallArg
EvaluateArgs
ExprEvaluatorBase<RecordExprEvaluator>::handleCallExpr
clang::VarDecl::checkForConstantInitialization
```

The evaluator frames leading to the fault are in `ExprConstant.cpp`.

## Additional information

The same code compiles successfully when the header is included textually,
without a PCH. A trivial `consteval` function defined in the PCH does not
crash; the failure requires the PCH-defined function to call
`std::meta::members_of`.

This was found in the project while compiling reflection-heavy code and
also reproduces through clangd's precompiled-preamble path. The standalone
reproducer does not require clangd.

Attached is the complete stderr output. I also have the crash handler's
auto-generated preprocessed source and run script available if they would be
useful.

## Summary

Both operator-symbol tables in libc++'s `<meta>` — `symbol_of(operators)` and `u8symbol_of(operators)` — spell the entry for `op_caret_equals` as `"^"`, duplicating the plain-xor entry instead of `"^="`. Every other compound assignment is correct.

```cpp
#include <meta>
#include <string_view>

static_assert(std::meta::symbol_of(std::meta::operators::op_caret_equals)
              == std::string_view("^="));    // fails: returns "^"
static_assert(std::meta::u8symbol_of(std::meta::operators::op_caret_equals)
              == std::u8string_view(u8"^=")); // fails: returns u8"^"
```

## Where

`libcxx/include/meta`, the `op_names` tables in `symbol_of` and `u8symbol_of`: the entry between `"%="` and `"&="` reads `"^"` in both tables.

## How we hit it

Found by a reflection-driven binding generator that renders C++ source text from reflections: for `absl::int128`'s `operator^=`, the generated source called `self.operator^(...)` — a non-existent member — and failed to compile. Code that *splices* the reflected function never notices; only consumers that render operator names textually (code generators, diagnostics, logging) see it, which is presumably why it has survived: `operator_of` and the enumerator are correct, only the symbol table row is off.

## Fix

One-line data fix in each table (`"^"` → `"^="` / `u8"^"` → `u8"^="`), plus a regression test asserting the full compound-assignment row of both tables. PR follows.

body:
Tracking issue for a series of reflection bugs found by exercising clang-p2996 against real-world C++ libraries (nlohmann/json, Abseil, TartanLlama/expected, spdlog, Eigen) through an automated reflection-driven Python binding generator. Each entry below links a self-contained issue (minimized repro) and a PR (fix + regression test under `libcxx/test/std/experimental/reflection/` or `clang/test/Reflection/`). Filing this so the set is reviewable as a whole — the bugs cluster into a few recurring root-cause families, and a couple of the mangler PRs stack.

### A. Reflection identity & equality

- [x] #302 / PR #305 — reflections of a **re-opened namespace** compare unequal across redeclarations (`parent_of(^^member) != ^^ns`). `profileReflection` profiled the raw decl pointer for `ReflectionKind::Namespace`; the `Template` case already canonicalized. Found via Eigen (`Eigen::internal` is re-opened in nearly every header).

### B. Sugar-blind metafunctions (same family, different sites)

- [x] #292 / PR #293 — **function-type** queries blinded by `AttributedType` sugar (`[[clang::lifetimebound]]` on accessors): qualifier predicates silently false, `return_type_of`/`parameters_of` reject the type. Found via Abseil (`ABSL_ATTRIBUTE_LIFETIME_BOUND`).
- [x] #304 / PR #307 — **`is_complete_type`** blinded by alias sugar: `findTypeDecl` on a `TypedefType` returns the alias decl, `EnsureInstantiated` no-ops, and an instantiable spec named through an alias reads incomplete (order-dependently). Found via spdlog (alias-heavy seeds and member typedefs).
- [x] #322 / PR #324 — **parameter-name queries depend on instantiation state**: the P3096 consistency walk ran over the instantiation's redeclaration chain, which member-definition instantiation collapses in place — `identifier_of(parameters_of(f)[0])` flipped between the declaration's and the definition's name depending on whether the definition had been instantiated, so two TUs reflecting the same entity disagreed. Now walks the template pattern's chain. Found via Eigen (`setConstant`: declared `value`, defined `val`) — the only surface mismatch across the corpus's two generated binding modules.

### C. Member / namespace enumeration (`members_of`)

- [ ] #290 / PR #291 — **entity-proxy** reflections hit `llvm_unreachable` in six member metafunctions and crashed the mangler (operator-named `using` shadows; identical mangling for overload sets behind one using-declarator). Found via Abseil `StatusOr` (`value()` re-exported from a private base).
- [x] #296 / PR #297 — reflection-triggered completion used **explicit-instantiation-definition semantics**, eagerly instantiating member bodies and wrong-rejecting specializations with lazily-ill-formed members (the specialized-storage-base idiom), order-dependently. Found via `tl::expected<void, E>`.
- [ ] #303 / PR #306 — a re-opened namespace block beginning with an **out-of-line class-member definition** derails the namespace walk: the definition pattern is yielded as a "member" (its reflection then crashes display/mangling) and every remaining member is silently dropped. Found via Eigen (69 of 125 namespace members survived).

- [ ] #313 / PR #317 — **silent truncation**: `members_of` stops at the implicit tag of `extern "C" { typedef struct X X; }` (semantic ctx = enclosing scope, lexical ctx = the linkage block; the semantic-chain step walks backward out of the block and ends the enumeration). Field impact: `Python.h`'s `pytypedefs.h` made **every global declared after it invisible to reflection** — a bound library's global free operators silently never bound. Stacks on PR #306.

### D. Itanium mangling of reflection NTTPs

- [ ] #286 / PR #287 — same-named **function-template** reflections as NTTPs mangled identically; CodeGen silently folded `linkonce_odr` instantiations (one body served both call sites, no diagnostic). Found via Abseil `flat_hash_map` (`operator[]` + its SFINAE-false lifetimebound pack sibling).
- [ ] #298 / PR #299 (stacks on #287) — **deduction-guide** reflections hit `llvm_unreachable("Can't mangle a deduction guide name!")` when lifted into mangled-name position. Found via `tl::unexpected`'s implicit guide.
- [ ] #300 / PR #301 (stacks on #299) — same-headed **member-template** reflections of a specialization mangled identically: `ODRHash::AddFunctionDecl` no-ops in "specialization context", so the #287 discriminator degenerated to the shared template head. Found via `tl::expected`'s four `value()` overloads (silent fold; caught only by differential testing).

- [ ] #312 / PR #316 — deduction-guide **SPECIALIZATION** reflections (Declaration kind, via `substitute` on the guide template) ICE through `mangleFunctionEncoding` → `mangleUnqualifiedName` ("Can't mangle a deduction guide name!") — the Declaration-kind sibling of #298. Stacks on PR #301.
- [ ] #314 / PR #318 — LP64 long-element NEON vectors ("unexpected Neon vector element type"): Darwin predeclares `__Int64x1_t` et al. with plain `long` elements; reflection's enumeration of TU members makes mangling such specializations routine. Likely reproducible in upstream clang.

body:
P2996 [expr.eq]: two reflections compare equal if they designate the same entity. For namespaces this fails across redeclarations:

```cpp
namespace c { namespace d {} }
namespace c { namespace d { template <class T> struct R {}; } }  // re-opened

static_assert(std::meta::parent_of(^^c::d::R) == ^^c::d);   // fails
```

`^^c::d` wraps the namespace's first `NamespaceDecl`, while `parent_of(^^c::d::R)` wraps the `NamespaceDecl` of the re-opened block that declared `R`. Reflection equality goes through `APValue::Profile` → `profileReflection` (`clang/lib/AST/APValue.cpp`), whose `ReflectionKind::Namespace` case profiles the raw declaration pointer — different redeclarations profile differently, so the reflections compare unequal. Single-block namespaces are unaffected (only one decl exists), which is why this is easy to miss: every `parent_of(...) == ^^ns` test in simple code passes.

The `ReflectionKind::Template` case in the same switch already canonicalizes (`getCanonicalDecl()`) for exactly this reason — `Namespace` looks like the gap.

Field shape where this bites: Eigen re-opens `Eigen::internal` in nearly every header, so an enclosing-namespace classification of the form `parent_of(template_of(spec)) == ^^Eigen::internal` silently answers false for essentially every entity in that namespace.

Note the alias distinction must survive a fix: a `NamespaceAliasDecl` is also carried under `ReflectionKind::Namespace`, and `^^alias != ^^ns` while `underlying_entity_of(^^alias) == ^^ns`. Canonicalizing each decl to its own first declaration preserves that (an alias's canonical decl is still the alias).

PR with a one-line fix (plus a regression test covering re-opened, doubly-nested, and alias shapes) to follow.

body:
## Summary

`members_of` over a namespace enumerates deduction guides like any other member. Lifting that member list into static storage with `define_static_array` gives the backing array specialization a linkage name in which each element reflection is mangled as a template argument (`CXXNameMangler::mangleReflection`). A reflection of a *template* is encoded by the template's name (`mangleTemplateName` → `mangleTemplatePrefix` → `mangleUnqualifiedName`) — but a deduction guide's `DeclarationName` is `CXXDeductionGuideName`, which has no `<unqualified-name>` encoding:

```
Can't mangle a deduction guide name!
UNREACHABLE executed at clang/lib/AST/ItaniumMangle.cpp:1774
  #8 CXXNameMangler::mangleUnqualifiedName
  #9 CXXNameMangler::mangleTemplatePrefix
 #10 CXXNameMangler::mangleTemplateName
 #11 CXXNameMangler::mangleReflection
```

That unreachable is a perfectly sound invariant for normal symbol mangling (guides are never odr-used) — but reflection makes guide *reflections* reachable in mangled-name position from ordinary user code.

A wrinkle that shapes the fix: once CTAD has been used in the TU, Sema's **implicit** guides (per-constructor + the copy guide) are enumerated alongside explicit ones, every guide for one template shares the single `CXXDeductionGuideName`, and an implicit per-constructor guide can be *structurally identical* to a same-signature explicit guide — so the encoding must discriminate all of them, not just avoid the crash.

## Field evidence

TartanLlama/expected v1.3.1 declares at namespace scope (always on at C++26):

```cpp
template <class E> unexpected(E) -> unexpected<E>;   // behind #ifdef __cpp_deduction_guides
```

A reflection-driven binding generator walks `members_of(parent_of(^^T))` through `define_static_array` while binding ANY class in `tl`, so every `tl::expected`/`tl::unexpected` binding ICEs at codegen (exit 134). There is no consumer-side dodge: the guide is unconditionally in the namespace.

## Reproducer

Self-contained, `-std=c++26 -freflection-latest`:

```cpp
#include <experimental/meta>

namespace demo {
template <class E> struct unexpected { unexpected(E); };
#ifdef GUIDE
template <class E> unexpected(E) -> unexpected<E>;
#endif
}

void walk() {
  template for (constexpr auto m :
      std::define_static_array(std::meta::members_of(
          ^^demo, std::meta::access_context::unchecked()))) {
    constexpr bool t = std::meta::is_template(m);
    static_assert(t || !t);
  }
}

int main() { walk(); }
```

Build matrix:

- `clang++ -DGUIDE -c repro.cpp` — **ICE** (the bug; needs codegen)
- `clang++ -c repro.cpp` — clean (control: no guide)
- `clang++ -DGUIDE -fsyntax-only` — clean (the front-end is fine; it is the mangler)

## Expected

Compiles and runs; each guide reflection gets a deterministic, distinct mangling.

## Actual (at `837da39eb88c`)

The unreachable above, exit 134.

## Suggested fix (PR follows shortly)

Local to `mangleReflection`'s `ReflectionKind::Template` case (the `mangleUnqualifiedName` unreachable stays): encode `"dg"` + the *deduced* template's name + the same `'$'`-bracketed ODR-hash discriminator used for overloaded function templates (#286), with `isImplicit()` and the deduction-candidate kind folded into the hash so explicit guides, same-signature implicit per-constructor guides, and copy guides all stay pairwise distinct. Deterministic and cross-TU-stable, preserving legitimate linkonce_odr merging; distinct from a reflection of the deduced class template itself. The regression test pins the lift shape plus four guides (2 explicit + 2 implicit) as `&probe<m>` NTTPs and asserts pairwise distinctness at runtime.

Note: the PR stacks on #287 (it extends the same `mangleReflection` hash block).

**Describe the bug**
The compiler rejects evaluation of `&value->[:field:]` when evaluating via `__builtin_is_within_lifetime`, claiming it is not a valid constant expression, despite `&static_cast<const Value&>(*value).[:field:]` compiling fine.

**To Reproduce**
See [this example](https://godbolt.org/z/asbqxnYhb) on compiler explorer.

**Expected behavior**
Both cases work as intended.

_Note: after writing, it appears that this issue not related to `__builtin_is_within_lifetime`, but rather applies generally to all constant evaluation and in most situations where the std::meta::info is computed in a non-trivial manner, not just when passing via nttp_

**Describe the bug**
https://godbolt.org/z/6d3hfEaPn has a very simple reproduction of the issue. There are three modules in the setup (excluding `std`):
* `annotate`, which introduces a tag used in the annotation
* `type`, which imports `annotate` and declares a type with a data member annotated by a tag from it
* `library`, which emulates some library code that checks for said annotation in some type's data member

**To Reproduce**

Code is in the Gobolt link

**Expected behavior**

The code compiles and outputs `true`

**Additional context**

Removing the annotation from `type.cppm` in the Godbolt makes the program compile fine and output `false` (as expected). Replacing `import annotate` with `export import annotate` in different places and/or adding `import annotate` to `main.cc` does not fix the issue in the Godbolt, but I've found the changes like this on my personal machine lead to the problem sometimes disappearing and then refusing to present itself even after the changes are reverted (similarly, on the real code I'm writing the "fixes" are just as non-persistent - not production code, of course, but the real project I wanted to try my hand on with reflection).

The meta context is `unchecked` because leaving it `current` would cause another compiler crash - although I assume it is to be expected since `library` would need to import `type` in order to have in-context access to `^^S`? I'm pretty sure incorrect access context is not the problem with this particular issue since manually providing the call site's access context (https://godbolt.org/z/nsKd84EYo - you can see I also changed some `import`s to `export import`s and even added `export import std` just to maybe get the code to compile and reveal the issue's unstable nature) still does not fix the compiler crash.

body:
**Describe the problem**
```cpp
#include <meta>

using namespace std::meta;

// error: cannot take the reflection of a using-declarator
static_assert(^^int == dealias(^^std::int32_t));
//                               ^

// https://eel.is/c++draft/meta.reflection#queries-55 example - passes
using X = int;
using Y = X;
static_assert(dealias(^^int) == ^^int);
static_assert(dealias(^^X) == ^^int);
static_assert(dealias(^^Y) == ^^int);
```

https://godbolt.org/z/he38aea4K

---

**Context**

https://eel.is/c++draft/meta.reflection#queries-55

```
[Example [5](https://eel.is/c++draft/meta.reflection#queries-example-5): 
using X = int;
using Y = X;
static_assert(dealias(^^int) == ^^int);
static_assert(dealias(^^X) == ^^int);
static_assert(dealias(^^Y) == ^^int);
— end example]
```

Reflecting a non-qualified name like `X`/`Y` works fine, as P2996 obviously allows reflecting a type alias and they are resolved usings.

However, `^^std::int32_t` causing an error has made me quite confused so I looked into what's happening.

---

From https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.reflect 

```
reflect-expression:
    ^^ ::
    ^^ reflection-name
    ^^ type-id
    ^^ id-expression
reflection-name:
    nested-name-specifier_opt identifier
    nested-name-specifier template identifier
```

https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.reflect#3 says 

> A reflect-expression is parsed as the longest possible sequence of tokens that could syntactically form a reflect-expression. An unparenthesized reflect-expression that represents a template shall not be followed by <.

I believe `nested-name-specifier` includes a namespace/namespace alias per

https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.prim.id.qual#nt:nested-name-specifier
https://eel.is/c++draft/namespace.def.general#nt:namespace-name

So `std::int32_t` _should_ be reflectable because it supposedly constitutes a `[namespace(-alias)]::[typedef-name]`.

---

However, turned out I guessed it wrong.

In `<cstdint>` those types are introduced by

```cpp
#include <stdint.h>
//...
_LIBCPP_BEGIN_NAMESPACE_STD
using ::int32_t _LIBCPP_USING_IF_EXISTS;
//...
_LIBCPP_END_NAMESPACE_STD
```

and alike. They are `using` decls importing types from another namespace rather than type aliases. And `libc++` is quite inconsistent about how to import types.

- `<cstdint>` -> `using ::T`
- `<__cstddef/max_align_t.h>` -> `using ::max_align_t`
- `<__cstddef/nullptr_t.h>` -> `using nullptr_t = decltype(nullptr);`
- `<__cstddef/ptrdiff_t.h>` -> `using ptrdiff_t = decltype(...);`
- so on and so on.

All I can say is this looks like a mess, and not being able to reflect `^^std::int32_t` is quite weird.

---

In Sema there are three possible locations where this error (`diag::err_reflect_using_declarator`) could be emitted:

- `Sema::BuildCXXReflectExpr` x2 overloads
- `Sema::ActOnCXXReflectExpr`

All of them are related to `UsingShadowDecl`/`UsingType` + `EntityProxyReflection`.

`UsingShadowDecl`/`UsingType` w/o `EntityProxyReflection` -> `err_reflect_using_declarator`

So types like `std::int32_t` are trapped perfectly because they are indeed `using_declarator`s.

---

I believe this is an issue that should be addressed. `^^std::int32_t` seems so innocent but it simply doesn't work. Again, this feels very weird. Should we make any attempt to unify the methods for defining types inside `std` namespace? How should we evaluate the impact of doing so? Has this issue been discussed by anybody anywhere? Input appreciated.

comments.body: For the code you pointed out in cstdint, they implement `std::int32_t` with `using ::int32_t`, which is a `using-declaration`, its different from something like `using X = int`, which is a `alias-declaration`.  The standard forbids applying reflection on `using declaration`, for now. https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.reflect#5.1

@changkhothuychung Yes, that's my point.

I am aware of the facts that

> they implement std::int32_t with using ::int32_t, which is a using-declaration

>The standard forbids applying reflection on using declaration

My point is that not being able to reflect `^^std::int32_t` is simply absurd.

In https://eel.is/c++draft/cstdint.syn#1 you can see

```
namespace std {
  using int8_t         = signed integer type;   // optional
  using int16_t        = signed integer type;   // optional
  using int32_t        = signed integer type;   // optional
  using int64_t        = signed integer type;   // optional
  using intN_t         = see below;             // optional
...
```

https://eel.is/c++draft/cstdint.syn#3

> All types that use the placeholder N are optional when N is not 8, 16, 32, or 64. The exact-width types intN_t and uintN_t for N = 8, 16, 32, and 64 are also optional; however, if an implementation defines integer types with the corresponding width and no padding bits, it declares the corresponding **typedef-names**. Each of the macros listed in this subclause is defined if and only if the implementation declares the corresponding **typedef-name**.
> [Note 1: The macros INTN_C and UINTN_C correspond to the **typedef-names** int_leastN_t and uint_leastN_t, respectively. — end note]

The Synopsis specified typedefs, the wording in the spec indicates that things should be typedefs. But **none** of `libc++`, `libstdc++` (https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-4.6.3/libstdc++/api/a00831_source.html), and MSVC does that. They all write like `using ::int32_t`.

Why? Is there any particular reason they are doing so or is this just some legacy before static reflection is a thing?

When people try to `^^std::int32_t` and figure they can't with any of the stblibs, but that the spec indicates it should work... How'd they think?

Before P2996, `using ::int32_t` and `using int32_t = ::int32_t` probably won't make much of a difference. But with P2996 in place, this is no longer the case.

And this is not a wording thing, because the spec is consistent. According to https://eel.is/c++draft/cstdint.syn and https://eel.is/c++draft/expr.reflect `^^std::int32_t` _should_ work. It might be that the stdlib implementers just used some equivalents to `using int32_t = ...` in the pre-C++26 era. So I consider this a library implementation bug that is inconsistent with P2996.

Should we patch the corresponding headers in libc++? If you think doing so makes sense, I can prepare PR.

I see.

> For the implementation of std::int32_t and other integer types with specified widths...

I have no issue with this part.

> Also, in the standard, it says that in C++, standard libraries need to be defined within the std namespace.

Nor with this.

> The reason why C++ doesn't have reflection on using-declaration yet is because the committee needs to decide what this means.

This is not my point here. P2996 has made itself clear that it wants to control its scope and leave more advanced features to future revisions of C++, e.g., extending `define_aggregate` etc. It also forbids splicing the ctors/dtors. I think not being able to reflect a `using declaration` is fine, since for your `^^D::fn` example to work, the `^^` operator essentially has to be able to reflect an overload set or so, even containing ambiguous names, and this is obviously not something P2996 is trying to do at the moment (though I hope that in the future we could be able to reflect an overload set of functions, etc.)

---

The problem, as you have pointed out, lies in here:

> Except as noted in [library] through [exec] and [depr], the contents of each header cname is the same as that of the corresponding header name.h as specified in the C standard library. In the C++ standard library, however, the declarations (except for names which are defined as macros in C) are within namespace scope of the namespace std. **It is unspecified whether these names (including any overloads added in [support] through [exec] and [depr]) are first declared within the global namespace scope and are then injected into namespace std by explicit using-declarations ([namespace.udecl]).**

- On the one hand, https://eel.is/c++draft/requirements#headers-5 says whether `injected into namespace std by explicit using-declarations` is **unspecified**. So probably the stdlib implementers just took the shortcut.
- On the other hand, the synopsis of `<cstdint>` etc writes in type aliases.

Pre-C++26, this might not make much of a difference and thank you for your input I now recognize this is not an implementation bug. But since P2996 has made itself into C++2c, could this be a wording conflict they overlooked?

To get things consistent, P2996 has made significant efforts in updating the wordings in many core language sections. But regarding libraries, it seems it is mainly concerned with adding the `<meta>` header.

---

> I agree that applying a reflection on std::int32_t should work.

Thank you for your consensus. Do you think that this is something P2996 should address, to make sure that those type names under `std::` have a defined way of introduction, instead of being _unspecified_ how they are defined in `std`? In my opinion this should be addressed, but I don't know where to raise this concern.

Sure, I do understand your rationale and perspective. When considering the ROI, a working older fork always wins over a shiny, broken piece. If we say, "Holy, clang 22 is out, let's merge it!" That's not development, that's losing mind getting high after caffeine overdosing. (Just joking)

---

If you don't mind, I'd like to dump some of my personal context and opinions here for you to reference.

Actually, as an indie gamedev, I've been watching over the C++ reflection thing for many years. After all, which gamedev would like to write tons of boilerplate wrappers, black magic macros, and even a customized build system with an own LLVM fork just to get script binding and rendering pipeline binding work intelligently? Devs want things got standardized.

Maybe in a span stretching long enough to about 10 years, proposals after proposals were raised concerning static reflection and got rejected again and again and again. The syntax, the motivations, the wordings, and how to implement things have been discussed until even now. One of the reasons why those proposals got rejected might be C++ is simply too big a beast, everyone looks at it differently, and another reason might be that the other foundations like `consteval`, `concept`s, and other metaprogramming things were simply not ready to support such a big introduction of static reflection.

The first _experimental_ implementation which caught my eye was lock3's clang fork. It has some sort of reflection abilities, code injections. But more it provided were ICEs. (I am not saying lock3's implementation was bad. It was a good attempt, just that several years ago things were in more dark an age than now.)

I understand that, this fork, was initiated as an _experimental_ fork exploring P2996 because it is something finally made into C++2c. And of course, no sane person would say "We are going to make the best P2996 implementation. Just try it out. Production ready." That's inviting legal issues and all. We know that not all features have been implemented; there are still ICEs, and behaviors not compliant with the spec.

However, the way I look it, this fork has grown to a point that it is more than just an experiment. When I opened P2996 and godbolt.org and realized that 14 out of 15 code examples provided in the proposal actually compile and work with this fork, the only conclusion I can have is "this is something worth a try." And it has been proving itself.

Maybe you think "for the community to test reflection in a meaningful way" primarily means coding in godbolt.org and seeing whether the compiler crashes. But as an indie gamedev who embraces the "Don't Repeat Yourself" (DIY) principle, I thought "screw it, let's see how far we can go."

Currently, I've been working on using static reflection with your fork to bind C++ functions with gameplay script virtual machine etc., a classic problem gamedevs hate so much because you gotta go through every class, function, parameter, and all, just to tell the vm that "things are there", even when there are binding libraries which help you do these sort of task, partially.

Obviously, this is not something that would be contained in several source files. My setup is MSBuild+ClangCL+your clang fork+libc++ if you wonder. This is a layered project. I started with looking at `<meta>` header thinking "the hell is this" and progressed to writing some reflection helpers, then went to higher-level things which handle the function reflection & binding & all.

And you know what? This fork holds. It might crash in rare cases, it might omit `closure::operator()`, but once the code is compiled, the program runs. `template for` works, `consteval` blocks work, most of the reflective metafunctions work exactly as specified in the wording. The implementation code looks solid (though it would be even better if you'd like to write some more comments :) ). It handles a certain scale of a project and its full potential is not yet known. I am still exploring it, that's why I have posted many issues, some just noting/asking things though. I hope that won't bother you so much. If so, please tell me.

This is why I think even LLVM is a moving target, and maybe LLVM mainstream is trying to implement reflection (are they really? I saw more commits about CUDA than about reflection. Maybe I should have a deeper look into its status.) It's because this fork is a _good one_. So I believe it deserves catching up with the upstream in other aspects.

In the upstream from clang 21 to 22, it seems like they have made some refactoring regarding Sema, templates (substitutions/maybe even treating concepts as a special kind of template, not yet sure about this/coding style changes/namespaces refactoring/etc.) But for real, I didn't see obvious signs of active development of static reflection underway. This fork is still, at this time point, the one that works, matches a specific level of expectation, able to hold a Visual Studio solution with tens of projects. Saying "we are still an experimental fork" might be too humble IMO. I am not familiar with GCC or so since I don't think it would work with MSBuild so I can't really test it.

But of course, keeping it working and working great should always be the top priority :)

---

Regarding my merging attempt, just regard that as my personal learning process. I will keep trying to probe the potential of this fork and give you heads-ups when I can. But if, out of the 1/100 possibility, I am somehow able to merge it, I will try to test it and maybe make a PR or so. But just don't expect it lol. I am really new to this thing.

To be honest, if I am left to deal with a giant like LLVM, especially considering that the upstream goes really fast, and to modify it in order to add functionalities and all, maybe I'd take a layered approach.

Simply changing the code on the forked branch is susceptible to large scale upstream refactoring just like the situation we are in now, resulting in massive conflicts and broken file change histories.

Maybe I'd do it the other way around: keep the main branch as-is, and maintain several feature branches that contain our own changes. Maybe like this:

- bloomberg-reflection-common (inc. enums/new common types/etc.)
- bloomberg-reflection-ast (inc. changes to AST reader/writer/context/etc.)
- bloomberg-reflection-sema-common
- bloomberg-reflection-sema-decl-expr
- bloomberg-reflection-sema-templates
- bloomberg-reflection-namespaces
- ...

Each holds parts of the whole reflection features, and all merged to something like `bloomberg-reflection-latest-dev`

And on that branch, active dev commits are made and cherry-picked to relevant feature branches.

When a merge from upstream is desirable, checkout each of the feature branches and, duplicate it. Try to rebase to the upstream or merge from the upstream and resolve the conflicts.

After all things clear, merge everything back to the dev branch. 

Well, I am not sure whether this approach would work here. At this point I don't think it worth the time to do this sort of thing. But I've been doing this with Epic's Unreal Engine (Epic's game engine if you are not familiar with them), I figure that this might be easier to manage when the upstream is changing fast.

Just some of my personal expreriences. Comments welcome, but don't have to :)

After looking into it, its because internally, this case, display_string_of will call return_type_of, and that's the function that keeps running forever for undeducible type - https://godbolt.org/z/Wq4zerbqh

However, looking at the spec for [return_type_of](https://eel.is/c++draft/meta.reflection#queries-66), I'm not sure whats the expected behavior when we call return_type_of on an undeducible type, should it throw meta::exception? @YukinoHayakawa
In this case I think `has-type` is false, and so we should throw @changkhothuychung ?

@changkhothuychung Here is some information I can provide:

1. After confirming with [CWG Jens Maurer](https://github.com/cplusplus/CWG/issues/827) (in this issue there might be some useful information I collected before) I am sure that
  - `auto func() { }` (deduced from function body)
  - `auto func() -> void` (trailing type)
  - non-generic lambdas' `operator::()`
All of them *do not* have undeduced placeholder type (i.e. `auto`) in their functions' types. As soon as the return type can be deduced, the `auto` is gone. The only occasion where `auto` remains in a function's type is a declaration `auto func();` *without any* clue for how to deduce its type. Note that we are not talking about anything involving template function here, i.e. functions with template params/auto type params.
2. By inspecting Sema's source code, I noticed that lambdas are somehow handled diffrently than ordinary functions. As far as I remember that's in `ActOnFunctionBodyFinish` or something like that (I can't open my Visual Studio properly at this moment so sorry I don't remember the exact function name. But I believe you know the function I am talking about.) Sema may wrap another layer of wrapper caller around a lambda's `operator()`. Maybe this is why writing `auto func() -> void {}` in a `struct` would cause it to appear in `members_of` but `[]() -> void {}` doesn't work in the same way. This is definitely a bug (#218, #219). We know that Sema's `getReturnType` is only filled when a function's return type is deduced, so technically `^^type_of` should cause side-effects on the the results of `members_of` but you are using `getDeclaredReturnType` to decide which functions are [`Q-members-of-representable`](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2025/p2996r13.html#pnum_676) This is NOT spec-compliant.
3. Getting back to whether `auto func();` has a type, well, it does have a type. @zebullax See [how cppreference says](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/function.html#:~:text=determining%20function%20type) about a function's type:
> In syntax (2), assuming noptr-declarator as a standalone declaration, given the type of the qualified-id or unqualified-id in noptr-declarator as “derived-declarator-type-list T” (T must be auto in this case):` (since C++11)
> If the exception specification is non-throwing, the type of the function declared is “derived-declarator-type-list noexcept function of parameter-type-list cv ﻿(optional) ref ﻿ ﻿(optional) returning trailing ﻿”. (since C++17)
> Otherwise, the(since C++17) type of the function declared is “derived-declarator-type-list function of parameter-type-list cv ﻿(optional) ref ﻿ ﻿(optional) returning trailing ﻿”. attr, if present, applies to the function type. (since C++11)

Well, if you let me say, this is even harder to understand than the wordings in P2996 so let's get back to the proposal.

4. The proposal says:

`consteval bool has-type(info r); // exposition only`
[1](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2025/p2996r13.html#pnum_527)Returns: true if r represents a value, object, variable, function whose type does not contain an undeduced placeholder type and that is not a constructor or destructor, enumerator, non-static data member, unnamed bit-field, direct base class relationship, or data member description. Otherwise, false.

So yes, a function can A. **has a type with a placeholder type** *and* B. **does not qualify as `has-type`** in P2996. By this wording, we can deduce that, even though I am not a C++ spec expert, that a function *can* have a type which contains `auto`. Otherwise, the wording in the proposal makes no sense.

Then, let's get to another section: 

[[meta.reflection.member.queries] Reflection member queries
](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2025/p2996r13.html#meta.reflection.member.queries-reflection-member-queries)

blahblahblah...

> A declaration D of a member M of a class or namespace Q is Q-members-of-eligible if ...
> A member M of a class or namespace Q is Q-members-of-representable from a point P if a Q-members-of-eligible declaration of M members-of-precedes P and M is ...
> a variable or reference V for which the type of V **does not contain an undeduced placeholder type**,
> a function F for which, ... the type of F **does not contain an undeduced placeholder type**,

**So I believe you are correct, @changkhothuychung , per P2996, a function whose type has a placeholder type not yet deduced does not qualify as `has-type` (in the context of P2996).** And `std::meta::type_of` should *NOT* return an object for it, because [`consteval info type_of(info r);` `Constant When: has-type(r) is true.` ](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2025/p2996r13.html#pnum_528).

**And @zebullax, I agree with that `std::meta::type_of` should throw for `auto func(); std::meta::typeof(^^func);`.**

And, I hope that the `members_of` problem could be fixed with this as well since it's not *that* hard to fix. You see, if `type_of` works fine for whatever functions/operators and your implementation of `type_of` simply desugars the return type, if the same has been done for `members_of` it should be easily fixed. Using `FD->getDeclReturnType()->isDeducedType()` is simply incorrect as per P2996. The deduced type should be used.

But Jens Maurer also [said](https://github.com/cplusplus/CWG/issues/827#issuecomment-3620005494):

> Note that for the second case, you might need to retain the "auto" return type in your compiler internals, even though it was already deduced, to properly perform declaration matching.

Well, at least `getDeclReturnType` is not hard in clang.

body:
I can see that this clang fork implements P3394 as it were specified at [R0](https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg21/docs/papers/2024/p3394r0.html), but already at R1 the API has been significantly reduced and that's what has been standardized.
To summarize the changes:

- `annotations_of` overload that takes an `item` and a `type` infos got renamed to `annotations_of_with_type`.
- `annotation_of` (singular) was dropped.
- `has_annotation` was dropped.
- `annotate` was dropped.

All that's left of annotations' synopsis is (from [R4](https://isocpp.org/files/papers/P3394R4.html) of the paper):

```
namespace std::meta {
  consteval bool is_annotation(info);

  consteval vector<info> annotations_of(info item);                      // (1)
  consteval vector<info> annotations_of_with_type(info item, info type); // (2)
}
```

Of course, I implement my own `annotations_of_with_type` and go on with my project, but I thought it would be good to mention this so this fork could actually match what was standardized.
title: Annotation API has changed in R1

Seems to trigger when:
- A templated entity (e.g., function template) contains a local templated context (i.e., expansion statement or generic lambda),
- A constant template parameter of the template entity has consteval-only type,
- That constant template parameter is named within the local templated context outside of an immediate function context.

Then the `DeclRefExpr` that names the constant template parameter is marked as an immediate-escalating expression during the instantiation of a specialization of the templated entity.

comments.body: Ah, interesting - it actually ICE's due to a failing assert when built with assertions (which the godbolt build is not).

So the right thing to do, I think, is for [`JumpScopeChecker::BuildScopeInformation`](https://github.com/bloomberg/clang-p2996/blob/p2996/clang/lib/Sema/JumpDiagnostics.cpp#L233-L247) to account for expansion statements. This is obnoxious though, because we end up diagnosing separately for both the dependent body of the expansion statement _and_ each expanded instantiation. That's because it gets triggered at function-end, after all expansions have taken place.

The way around that is to call `Sema::DiagnoseInvalidJumps` at the start of `FinishCXXExpansionStmt`, diagnose only the dependent body, and return `StmtError()` if a diagnostic was issued. The problem is that `DiagnoseInvalidJumps` doesn't actually surface whether a diagnostic was issued back to the caller, so there's not really a way to implement that (granted, I could check if _any_ diagnostics have been issued, but that's a pattern that's landed me in trouble before).

So I'm just gonna leave this open for now - Maybe I'll circle back and make `DiagnoseInvalidJumps` surface whether it issued a diagnostic, but there are already enough reflection-y things going on leading up to Sofia; this isn't a priority.
